Headline: Op Ed: Steve Clagg On Travel Programs As A Dead Node In Enterprise AI
Full Text:
As enterprises deploy AI orchestration systems, corporate travel programs risk becoming isolated without agent-callable, MCP-compatible architecture, warns consultant Steve Clagg. He calls on travel management pros to demand interoperability from suppliers — not just better interfaces — and join their organizations' AI strategy conversations as early as possible.

   Somewhere in a conference room, a CIO is presenting the company's enterprise AI roadmap. Slide after slide shows the new operating system being built beneath the business: Microsoft Copilot ecosystem, built on Azure AI Foundry, orchestrating employee requests; Salesforce Agentforce handling procurement approvals and contract routing; ServiceNow agents resolving IT tickets without a human touching them. The CFO leans in, impressed. The slide deck is genuinely beautiful. Someone asks about travel. The CIO pauses, pulls up the next slide and there it is: a box in the corner of the workflow diagram labeled "T&E," with exactly zero connections to anything else in the graph. It's not because they forgot; it's because the travel program had no architecture that could connect.

    

   At most companies, the travel program sits isolated, portal-based, traveler-facing and completely invisible to the enterprise AI layer being built above and around it. The people designing that AI layer are not waiting for your TMC to catch up.

    

   What is actually happening at the enterprise level matters more to a corporate travel director than anything their TMC has announced this year.

    

   The major enterprise software vendors have stopped selling AI features. They are selling AI operating systems. These aren't chatbots bolted onto existing software. They are orchestration layers: systems that can receive a business goal, decompose it into tasks, call other systems through standardized interfaces, manage approvals, trigger workflows and return a result — all without a human touching a keyboard. The enterprise is building an AI that can do things beyond answering questions.

    

   The Human-In-The-Loop Problem

    One of the protocols making this possible is MCP, the Model Context Protocol, which Anthropic released in late 2024 and which the Linux Foundation has since taken on as a governed open standard. Think of it as the USB port for enterprise AI, a standardized interface that lets any AI agent discover, connect to and take actions inside any system that exposes an MCP server.

    

   Turkish Airlines has already built one. Sabre (the GDS that has been powering, and occasionally tormenting, travel industry back-ends since the 1960s) launched its own MCP server in September 2025, explicitly positioning its inventory as callable infrastructure for any AI agent. The pipe got modernized, but the water is the same.

    

   Lumo is a more instructive example of what agent-ready travel intelligence can actually look like when it's built right. The company launched an MCP server that lets any enterprise AI agent pass in a live itinerary and get back as structured output flight disruption probability, connection risk with an explanation and rebooking recommendations. Ask it whether your traveler is going to make their connection in Dallas and it returns a probability score and a suggestion. That is decision-grade intelligence an enterprise agent can act on: trigger a rebooking workflow, alert the traveler and escalate to a travel counselor before the airport does it for you. No portal, no browser, just a callable service that makes the enterprise AI smarter about travel.

    

   The industry needs more of that. At most TMCs and OBTs, the architecture is not there to support it.

    

   Let's be honest about what most are actually building.

    

   SAP Concur announced the Joule AI assistant now integrates with Microsoft 365 Copilot so employees can create expense reports without leaving Microsoft applications. That is a real and useful thing. It also announced a booking agent that can generate itineraries aligned with company policy, which entered early adopter availability in late 2025.

    

   Navan's Ava assistant handles booking modifications, refunds and traveler profile updates, and reportedly handles tens of thousands of interactions per month.

    

   Amex GBT is rebuilding Egencia with "agentic AI search," and announced it is working on an agent-to-agent architecture with undisclosed major technology partners.

    

   BCD Travel partnered with Oversee to deploy agentic AI across operations and launched a chat-based assistant inside Slack and Microsoft Teams for bookings and itinerary changes. Last week, it announced MCP capabilities for its Tripsource platform and reported that a "few" customers were exploring it.

    

   Read all of that charitably and it sounds like real progress. Some of it is. But almost all of it is traveler-facing: AI that helps the human traveler book, modify or expense their trip. The Joule integration is essentially an embedded form that surfaces inside Microsoft 365 rather than a callable service that Copilot can invoke autonomously as part of a broader workflow. The BCD Slack integration is excellent for a traveler who messages a bot.

    

   A Slack bot answers a person who messages it. An enterprise AI agent is something other agents call programmatically, with structured inputs and outputs, as part of a graph of automated business processes. The distinction matters and most travel vendors are blurring it. Helping a traveler book faster is one thing; making travel callable by an enterprise AI system is another. The entire enterprise AI build-out is predicated on the second, and the travel industry is almost entirely focused on the first.

    

   The architectural problem is pretty straightforward. Enterprise AI platforms work by building a graph of callable services. When a Salesforce Agentforce agent books a client visit, ideally it should call a travel service; pass in the traveler profile, destination, policy parameters and budget ceiling; receive back a confirmed itinerary; trigger the approval workflow; and post the booking to the expense system. That chain of events requires every node in the graph to be agent-callable. It must accept structured requests from other agents, not just from humans typing into a portal.

    

   Most travel platforms today are built around the human-in-the-loop assumption. The interface is a browser. The user is the traveler. The AI, when it exists, assists that traveler in navigating the portal. The platform was never designed to be called by another piece of software autonomously, at machine speed, without a human clicking anything. When your company's enterprise AI team tries to include travel in their workflow graph, they run into a wall. The TMC's API, if it exists beyond basic data pulls, is not designed for agentic execution. The OBT has no MCP server. The booking confirmation lives in an email that nothing downstream can parse. And so, the enterprise AI team does what enterprise AI teams always do when they hit a wall: They route around it, treat travel as a manual exception and build the graph without you.

    

   This Isn't Theoretical

    It is happening right now at companies that are deploying Copilot Studio, Agentforce and ServiceNow AI agents. The IT teams building those platforms are not asking your TMC for help. They have never met your travel director. The travel director, in most organizations, has no seat on the enterprise AI strategy committee, no voice in the platform architecture decisions and no visibility into what is being built.

    

   Another view is that the travel procurement decision is separate from the AI strategy decision, that travel directors manage contracts and policy while IT builds the AI platform, and that these things can be reconciled later with an integration. This is the same argument people made for 20 years about travel and ERP systems, and the result is that most companies still have travel data that cannot be reliably connected to their general ledger without a manual process. "We'll integrate it later" is how you end up with a permanent dead node in the graph.

    

   Another version of the argument is that your TMC will handle it, that they are already building the agent-to-agent infrastructure and you just need to wait. Maybe. BCD's MCP announcement represents progress. Amex GBT is explicit about this direction, and its agent-to-agent framing at least shows it understands what is being asked. But "we are architecting an agent-to-agent approach and working with partners including a major technology company" is not the same as shipping product. It is a roadmap statement. In the meantime, your company's Copilot Studio deployment is not waiting. It is going live this quarter.

    

   Build It In Or Get Left Out

    What should a corporate travel director actually do with this? Don't just make a list, but execute a mindset shift and some practical pressure.

    

   Stop buying AI features and start buying for AI interoperability. When a TMC or OBT demos their AI assistant, the question is not, "Does it look impressive?" The question is, "Can an enterprise AI agent call this service without a human in the loop?" If the answer involves a portal, a traveler-facing chatbot or a browser session, that is not enterprise AI interoperability. That is a better user interface. Both are worth something, but only one belongs in your IT procurement criteria for 2026 and beyond.

    

   Ask your vendors: Do you have an MCP server? Do you support agent-to-agent API calls with structured responses? What is your roadmap for callable travel services within enterprise AI orchestration platforms? The vendors who can answer those questions are building the right things.

    

   Image: Steve Clagg, generated with NotebookLM When a TMC shows you a conversational booking interface and calls it AI, they are showing you a front-end improvement, which is fine, but they are not showing you infrastructure. Agent-facing architecture means your booking platform can receive a request from Copilot or Agentforce or ServiceNow, fulfill it against your policy and preferred supplier configuration, return a confirmed result in structured format and route the expense data to your ERP without a human touching anything. That is the architecture your enterprise AI team needs. If your TMC cannot describe how they are building it, you should be asking why.

    

   Travel is a workflow that touches almost every other business process. Sales team travel connects to CRM, procurement team travel to sourcing, conference attendance to marketing spend. If travel is not represented as a node in the enterprise workflow design, it will not be built in. Once the graph is finalized and the agents are deployed, adding travel later is an infrastructure retrofit, which is expensive and never a top priority. You need to be in that room with your company's AI strategy team before the graph is drawn.

    

   What does an agent-executed booking look like in your program? What policy parameters must be passable via API? What approval logic needs to be callable by a Copilot agent? What expense data needs to return in a format that your ERP agent can process without human intervention? These are procurement requirements, and they belong in your next RFP alongside fare performance benchmarks and duty of care capabilities. The vendors who respond with concrete architecture answers have thought about this. The vendors who respond with a brochure about their "AI-powered platform" have not. The question itself is the filter.

    

   Corporate travel has spent 20 years fighting to be recognized as a strategic function and not just an administrative one. The argument has always been that travel spend is material, travel data is strategic and travel policy is a business lever. That argument was always correct, but was always hard to win because the data was locked in portal silos, the program visibility was poor and the vendors had every incentive to keep it that way.

    

   Enterprise AI changes the stakes. The travel platform that wins the next decade is not the one with the best chatbot; it is the one that every enterprise AI orchestration layer knows how to call.

    

   Your TMC's AI demo isn't the point. What matters is whether your travel program exists in the enterprise graph at all.

Headline: Let's be clear about the value of an American Airlines hub in Charlotte | Opinion
Full Text:
Last month, the City of Charlotte announced a one-year extension to the renewal of the Airline Use and Lease Agreement with American Airlines and

   five other carriers operating at Charlotte Douglas International Airport. The agreement governs how an asset that supports $40 billion in annual economic output across North Carolina will be operated and improved over the next decade. It deserves the public's full attention and a fair-minded debate. So far, neither has been on offer.

    

    Recent advocacy from labor groups has drawn sweeping conclusions about Charlotte Douglas International Airport from narrow slices of data, painting American Airlines' 90 percent share of passenger traffic as evidence of pricing abuse and labor exploitation.

    

    The grievances themselves are not without merit. Wages for subcontracted cabin cleaners, wheelchair attendants, and other vendor employees deserve careful consideration, and the city's response that the lease agreement cannot legally govern subcontractor pay is a real constraint, not a brush-off.

    

    But the broader case being made against the hub itself overlooks the structural realities of operating a major connecting airport, and what those realities have meant for the Charlotte region.

    

    First, the hub makes CLT a powerful economic engine. A study from NC State University's Institute for Transportation Research and Education estimates that American's hub alone supports nearly 150,000 jobs across North Carolina and generates $30 billion in annual economic output. That includes direct airline employment as well as ripple effects from passenger spending at hotels, restaurants, rental cars, and local businesses.

    

    Second, decades of targeted infrastructure investment have delivered results. American has shouldered the largest share of landing fees and, through the current ten-year lease, supported more than $3 billion in capital improvements: a complete overhaul and expansion of the main terminal, the fourth parallel runway now under construction, concourse renovations, and 19 additional gates. These upgrades have improved the experience for everyone flying in and out of CLT, not just American's passengers.

    

    Third, CLT delivers genuine connectivity. CLT offers nonstop service to 194 destinations, more than twice the average for similarly sized non-hub metros like Nashville, Austin, and San Diego. Access to European markets is two to eight times greater than at comparable cities. Charlotte's airfares fall in the middle of the pack among the three major network carriers in comparable markets, and average fares here are actually lower today than they were before the pandemic, a claim few other major categories of consumer spending can make. Without the hub, the region would not get cheaper fares. It would get a fraction of the destinations.

    

    During the Global Financial Crisis, Wachovia, then Charlotte's largest private employer, collapsed and was acquired by Wells Fargo. Yet Charlotte came through the crisis with minimal net job losses in financial services, and Wells Fargo today employs more people in the region than in any other market. A core reason: CLT's robust air service enabled travel to the bank's other major operating centers without losing a workday. The same connectivity has played the same role in landing Honeywell, Truist, Sumitomo Mitsui, Pacific Life, Maersk, and Scout Motors in the years since.

    

    CLT's success was not accidental. Protecting that edge in 2026 will require timely decisions – not just on the airport lease, but on finding a credible path forward on the I-77 South toll lane project, a serious reset on development at Brooklyn Village, and numerous other economic questions.

Headline: US: 5th-gen VELA nuclear reactor fleet to get 3D-printed parts with new deal
Full Text:
Aman Tripathi  Industrial additive manufacturing is entering the commercial nuclear power sector through a new production agreement between two Midwestern companies.

   NX Atomics, an Indiana-based small modular reactor (SMR) developer, will utilize technology from Chicago's Sciaky to manufacture components for its upcoming reactor fleet. The agreement centers on integrating Sciaky's Electron Beam Additive Manufacturing (EBAM) process into the production line of NX Atomics' VELA reactor platform. NX Atomics is developing the fifth-generation VELA reactor to bypass traditional electrical grid infrastructure. Instead, the company is positioning the system to provide direct baseload electricity and high-temperature process heat to localized, power-intensive operations. The strategy is aimed directly at the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence data centers and heavy industrial facilities, with a target production cost of under $20/MWh. Overcoming cost barriers with advanced architecture Traditional nuclear energy projects frequently face economic hurdles due to the extensive lead times and high capital requirements of manufacturing heavy components. The partnership intends to alter this dynamic by replacing conventional fabrication methods with industrial 3D printing. Beyond faster initial production, the VELA platform introduces an unconventional operational model: rather than designing every internal component to endure for the entire lifecycle of the reactor, the system utilizes an interchangeable architecture. Certain parts are engineered to be systematically replaced during routine maintenance, which lowers initial manufacturing constraints and reduces long-term operational overhead. "This is what bringing nuclear manufacturing into the modern era actually looks like," said John Warden, CEO of NX Atomics. "3D printing opens up the potential for us to produce nuclear-qualified parts faster and at lower cost, where appropriate swap them out through life, and meaningfully reduce the unit cost of every small modular reactor we build." Transitioning proven aviation tech to energy infrastructure The production technique has already transitioned from experimental prototyping to standardized use in other heavy industries. Over the last ten years, aerospace and defense manufacturers have used the EBAM process to supply structural titanium and specialized alloy components for commercial aircraft, naval ships, and defense systems. The technology has also assisted space flight, providing printed propulsion elements for orbital platforms and lunar landing vehicles. "Our EBAM process produces parts that fly on commercial aircraft, sail on naval vessels, and orbit the earth," concluded John Criso, CEO of Sciaky. "Bringing that capability into America's clean energy infrastructure with NX Atomics is a natural next step, and we are proud that two Midwestern companies are leading this transition." US' advanced microreactor deployment plans In a separate domestic nuclear development, the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) has accepted a Construction Permit Application (CPA) to deploy NANO Nuclear Energy's KRONOS micro modular reactor at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (U. of I.). This acceptance transitions the project from the initial planning stage to a formal regulatory evaluation, allowing the NRC to begin its detailed technical, safety, and environmental reviews. The KRON O S reactor is a stationary, fourth-generation nuclear energy system built to provide carbon-free electricity and process heat directly to co-located infrastructure. In a single-unit layout, the installation generates up to 45 MWth of power, while multi-unit configurations can scale up to deliver gigawatt-level output. Designed to be transported by road and assembled directly on site, the modular system allows operators to deploy multiple units concurrently to expand capacity and reduce the levelized cost of electricity.

Headline: Auckland mega-projects: CBRE lists biggest new buildings under construction
Full Text:
New Zealand's largest new warehouse hub - a $1 billion-plus project near Auckland Airport - dominates the list of the city's 33 current or planned construction mega-projects.

    Zoltan Moricz, the Auckland-based head of research and executive director at CBRE, has released the latest new development pipeline report with colleague Roger Du.

    

    That listed all 33 large schemes where physical works have started or are imminent for office, retail and industrial buildings.

    

    Industrial is the powerhouse with 17 projects, followed by office with nine and retail with seven, according to the study

    

    By far the largest project is on a site being developed by James Kirkpatrick Group

    

    That is between Manukau City and Auckland Airport, near the State Highway 20 motorway ramps.

    

    Auckland's largest current development project was identified by CBRE as 65,000sq m of building works at 352-358 Puhinui Rd, opposite Manukau Memorial Gardens.

    

    The Herald has previously reported on the huge James Kirkpatrick Group scheme.

    

    352-358 Puhinui Rd

    

    Last November, CBRE listed 42 projects with some of the bigger active office and retail projects set for completion by year's end.

    

    CBRE data listed projects in the three sectors.

    

    Top 10 industrial projects

    

    358 Puhinui Rd, Wiri: 6.5ha floorspace by James Kirkpatrick Group;

    

    38-44 Dalgety Drive, Wiri, 3.1ha by ESR Australia & New Zealand;

    

    15 Maurice Paykel Place, East Tamaki, 2.7ha for Fisher & Paykel Healthcare;

    

    31 Prices Rd, Wiri, 25, 100sq m, Graeme Hart's Fernbrook Investments

    

    Te Kapua Drive, airport corridor, 2.4ha for Auckland International Airport;

    

    2 Monahan Rd, Mt Wellington, 2.1ha, Goodman;

    

    25 Druces Rd, Wiri, 1.9ha, ESR Australia & New Zealand;

    

    10 Te Ahurea St, Hobsonville, 1.7ha, Waide Construction

    

    11 Kirkbride Rd, airport corridor, 10,000sq m, Fife Capital;

    

    Spedding Rd, Whenuapai, 8500sq m, Calder Stewart.

    

    CBRE said Wiri, the airport corridor, and East Tamaki are the three most active precincts for industrial development.

    

    "In Wiri, James Kirkpatrick, Fernbrook and ESR are the only developers building warehouses, with a combined development size of over 140,000sq m, to date all without precommitment," it said.

    

    In the airport corridor, three projects are under construction, two of which are cold storage buildings.

    

    Auckland International Airport is building a 25,000sq m cold store for Foodstuffs.

    

    Fife Capital is developing a 10,000sq m building for Refrigafreighters on Kirkbride Rd.

    

    Top new retail projects

    

    56 Maki St, Westgate, 22,1200sq m by Mark Gunton's New Zealand Retail Property Group, new Kmart and other bulky format stores;

    

    44-48 Brigham Creek Rd, Whenuapai, 5500sq m, private developer;

    

    583 Te Atatu Rd, Massey, 3363sq m, ex-Woolworths becoming New World Te Atatu by Foodstuffs North Island;

    

    131 Queen St, CBD, 3000sq m, Andrew Krukziener's repurposing of existing building to create a new Faradays store

    

    Mt Wellington Highway, 1500sq m, Kiwi Property Group

    

    34-40 Queen St, 1500sq m, refurbishment of Queens Arcade by Davis Properties;

    

    "The retail development pipeline remains patchy. It includes Zone 6 large-format retail and 15 Maki Street in Westgate, a retail project on Brigham Creek Rd in Whenuapai and Kmart's new extension space in Sylvia Park," CBRE said.

    

    Queens Arcade and Faradays department store are to be completed in this year's second half in Auckland CBD.

    

    "Additionally, a few new supermarkets will be completed over the next two to three years across diverse locations. New World Te Atatu will be completed in this year's second half."

    

    Construction of Woolworths Onehunga is likely to start late this year, the research said.

    

    Top new office projects

    

    75-77 Remuera Rd, Newmarket , 8500sq m by Mansons TCLM

    

    9 Marewa Rd, Greenlane, 6350sq m, Clearwater Construction

    

    164 Beaumont St, CBD, 3320sq m, Orams Marine

    

    137 Great North Rd, Grey Lynn, 2625sq m, Samson Corporation;

    

    22-28 Customs St East, 2500sq m, Cooper and Company

    

    128-138 Parnell Rd, 1375sq m, Southbourne Holdings;

    

    288 Ponsonby Rd, 1000sq m, Triumph Capital;

    

    42 Ponsonby Rd, 974sq m, Samson Corporation.

    

    Three office projects in the CBD and four in non-CBD, mainly in the city fringe, are under construction, bringing 37,000sq m of new and refurbished space.

    

    Construction of the other two small buildings, totalling around 260sq m in the city fringe, will start soon.

    

    The biggest office project under construction is Bledisloe House at 24 Wellesley St West (13,000 sqm), followed by 75-77 Remuera Rd (8500sq m) and 9 Marewa Rd (6400sq m.

    

    Anne Gibson has been the Herald' s property editor for 26 years, written books and covered property extensively here and overseas.
